title: Isogeny degree is polynomial on finite rational endomorphism spans
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], and let $A/k$ be an abelian variety [def-sc-abelian-variety] of positive dimension $g$. Write $E=\operatorname{End}_k(A)$ for its group-scheme endomorphisms [def-sc-group-scheme] with pointwise addition and $E^0=E\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. For $a\in E$ define $d(a)$ to be the degree of $a$ if $a$ is an isogeny [def-sc-isogeny], and $0$ otherwise. There is a well-defined function $d^0:E^0\to\mathbf Q$ satisfying $d^0(a\otimes 1)=d(a)$ and $d^0(v)=n^{-2g}d(a)$ whenever $n>0$ and $nv=a\otimes1$. For every finite-dimensional rational subspace $V\subseteq E^0$ [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace] and every ordered rational basis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ of $V$, there is a homogeneous polynomial $P_e\in\mathbf Q[X_1,\ldots,X_r]$ of degree $2g$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], meaning that every nonzero monomial has total degree $2g$, and allowing the zero polynomial on a subspace, such that $d^0(\sum_i x_i e_i)=P_e(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ for all $x_i\in\mathbf Q$. In particular $P_e(0)=0$, and for every isogeny $a\in E$, $d^0(a\otimes1)=d(a)$ is a positive integer.

source.place: Chapter I, Remark 10.11, printed p.47, and Proposition 10.13 with its proof, printed pp.47–48; degree convention before Theorem 10.9, printed p.46. Homogeneous means every nonzero monomial has total degree 2g; zero restrictions are allowed.

proof.text:
Choose an ample invertible module $\mathcal H$ by [lem-sc-abelian-variety-projective] and put $\mathcal N=\mathcal H\otimes[-1]^*\mathcal H$. By [lem-sc-ample-tensor] this is ample and symmetric. The scheme $A$ is geometrically integral by [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization]. Put $c=(\mathcal N^g\cdot A)$. This equals the Hilbert degree: if $p(t)=\chi(A,\mathcal N^t)$, the coefficient of $n_1\cdots n_g$ in $p(n_1+\cdots+n_g)$ is $g!$ times its degree-$g$ coefficient. Thus [lem-sc-positive-ample-hilbert-degree] gives $c>0$. For every $a\in E$, [lem-sfb-equal-dimension-isogeny-criterion] and [lem-sfb-top-intersection-pullback] give
$$((a^*\mathcal N)^g\cdot A)=c\,d(a).$$
Indeed a nonisogeny is nondominant, giving zero; for an isogeny [lem-sc-isogeny-degree] identifies its finite-morphism degree with its kernel-order degree.

source.place: Proposition 10.13 proof, first displayed intersection equality, printed p.48

proof.text: For $n\geq1$, the homomorphism $na$ equals $[n]\circ a$. By [lem-sc-mult-n-pullback], $(na)^*\mathcal N\cong(a^*\mathcal N)^{\otimes n^2}$. Multilinearity [lem-sfb-top-intersection-multilinear] and step 1 give $d(na)=n^{2g}d(a)$. Symmetry of $\mathcal N$ gives $(-a)^*\mathcal N\cong a^*\mathcal N$, hence $d(-a)=d(a)$. For $a=0$ the pullback is a trivial invertible module (it factors through the identity point); its top intersection is zero since $g>0$. Thus $d(0)=0$ and $d(na)=n^{2g}d(a)$ for every integer $n$.

source.place: Remark 10.11, printed p.47; symmetric-module specialization of Proposition 10.13

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-rational-tensor-fractions], write $v=j(a)/n$ with $n>0$ and define $d^0(v)=n^{-2g}d(a)$. If also $v=j(b)/m$, then $j(ma)=j(nb)$; the same cited statement supplies $c>0$ with $cma=cnb$. Applying step 2 gives $(cm)^{2g}d(a)=(cn)^{2g}d(b)$, hence $n^{-2g}d(a)=m^{-2g}d(b)$. This proves independence without assuming finite generation or torsion-freeness of $E$. It also proves $d^0(j(a))=d(a)$ and, by choosing numerator and denominator for a rational scalar, $d^0(tv)=t^{2g}d^0(v)$ for $t\in\mathbf Q$, including $t=0$.

source.place: Remark 10.11, printed p.47: extension and independence of denominator

proof.text:
Fix $a,b\in E$ and use additive notation for isomorphism classes of invertible modules, where addition is tensor product and negation is dual. Put $C_n=[(na+b)^*\mathcal N]$ and $B=[(2a)^*\mathcal N]-2[a^*\mathcal N]$. Pull [thm-sc-theorem-of-cube] back along $(na+b,a,a):A\to A^3$. Its seven terms give
$$C_{n+2}-2C_{n+1}+C_n=B.$$
This holds for all $n\in\mathbf Z$. The sequence $\binom n2B+nC_1-(n-1)C_0$ has the same values at $0,1$ and the same second difference. Induction forwards from $0,1$ and backwards from $1,0$ therefore proves
$$C_n=\binom n2B+nC_1-(n-1)C_0\quad(n\in\mathbf Z).$$
Tensor inverses exist because the modules are invertible; the binomial coefficient is integral also for negative $n$.

source.place: Corollary 5.3, printed p.22; Proposition 10.13 recurrence and induction, printed p.48

proof.text:
Use rational multilinearity [lem-sfb-top-intersection-multilinear] to expand the $g$-fold intersection of $\binom T2B+TC_1-(T-1)C_0$ with itself, and divide by $c$. This is a polynomial $Q_{a,b}(T)\in\mathbf Q[T]$ of degree at most $2g$: every one of its $g$ factors contributes degree at most two. Steps 1 and 4 show $Q_{a,b}(n)=d(na+b)$ for all integers $n$. Fix $m>0$. At every integer $j$, step 2 gives $Q_{a,mb}(mj)=m^{2g}Q_{a,b}(j)$. Two univariate rational polynomials agreeing at infinitely many points are equal (a nonzero polynomial has at most its degree many roots). Hence $Q_{a,mb}(mT)=m^{2g}Q_{a,b}(T)$. At $t=p/m$, the definition of $d^0$ now gives
$$d^0(tj(a)+j(b))=m^{-2g}Q_{a,mb}(p)=Q_{a,b}(t).$$
For arbitrary $v,w\in E^0$, take a common positive denominator $h$ with $hv=j(a)$ and $hw=j(b)$ by [lem-sfb-rational-tensor-fractions]. It follows that $d^0(tv+w)=h^{-2g}Q_{a,b}(t)$ on all $\mathbf Q$. The bound $2g$ is uniform in $v,w$.

source.place: Proposition 10.13 proof, printed p.48: polynomial intersection expansion; Remark 10.11 denominator reduction made explicit

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-bounded-line-polynomial-interpolation] to $W=E^0$, $F=d^0$, $K=\mathbf Q$, and $D=2g$, using step 5. For each ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ of $V$, obtain $P_e\in\mathbf Q[X_1,\ldots,X_r]$ of total degree at most $2g$ with the required values. This includes $r=0$.

lean.statement: theorem IsAbelianVariety.exists_degree_polynomial {k : Type u} [Field k] (A : Over (Spec (.of k))) [GrpObj A] [IsAbelianVariety A] (hg : 0 < IsAbelianVariety.dim A) : ∃ (d : Additive (Grp.mk A ⟶ Grp.mk A) → ℚ) (d0 : ℚ ⊗[ℤ] Additive (Grp.mk A ⟶ Grp.mk A) → ℚ), (∀ a : Additive (Grp.mk A ⟶ Grp.mk A), (IsIsogeny a.toMul.hom.hom → d a = (isogenyDegree a.toMul.hom.hom : ℚ)) ∧ (¬ IsIsogeny a.toMul.hom.hom → d a = 0)) ∧ (∀ a : Additive (Grp.mk A ⟶ Grp.mk A), d0 (1 ⊗ₜ[ℤ] a) = d a) ∧ (∀ (v : ℚ ⊗[ℤ] Additive (Grp.mk A ⟶ Grp.mk A)) (n : ℕ), 0 < n → ∀ a : Additive (Grp.mk A ⟶ Grp.mk A), n • v = 1 ⊗ₜ[ℤ] a → d0 v = ((n : ℚ) ^ (2 * IsAbelianVariety.dim A))⁻¹ * d a) ∧ (∀ (V : Submodule ℚ (ℚ ⊗[ℤ] Additive (Grp.mk A ⟶ Grp.mk A))) [FiniteDimensional ℚ V] (r : ℕ) (e : Module.Basis (Fin r) ℚ V), ∃ P : MvPolynomial (Fin r) ℚ, P.IsHomogeneous (2 * IsAbelianVariety.dim A) ∧ (∀ x : Fin r → ℚ, d0 (V.subtype (∑ i : Fin r, x i • e i)) = MvPolynomial.eval x P) ∧ MvPolynomial.eval (0 : Fin r → ℚ) P = 0) ∧ (∀ a : Additive (Grp.mk A ⟶ Grp.mk A), IsIsogeny a.toMul.hom.hom → d0 (1 ⊗ₜ[ℤ] a) = (isogenyDegree a.toMul.hom.hom : ℚ) ∧ 0 < isogenyDegree a.toMul.hom.hom)
